question.leadin: He was killed near the end of a June 1876 battle in the Montana territory.
question.text: Name that 7th Cavalry commander famous for his "last stand."
question.clue: In one battle, this man decided not to wait for Alfred Terry's troops.

swap.text: This corrupt New York political machine supported many Democratic politicians during the late-19th and early-20th centuries. It was depicted as a ferocious tiger by political cartoonist Thomas Nast.
swap.clue: William Mooney was the first Grand Sachem of this group, that helped Al Smith secure the presidential nomination in 1928.

question.text: This women's rights advocate was not at Seneca Falls in 1848, though her parents and sister were there and signed the Declaration of Sentiments. In 1873, she was convicted and fined $100 -- a fine she refused to pay -- for voting while female.
question.clue: This woman is the alleged author of "Marriage and Maternity," an article published in The Revolution.

swap.text: In 1872, this editor of The New York Tribune split with Grant and was nominated to run against him by the Liberal Republican Party and the Democratic Party. He died between the election and the counting of the electoral votes.
swap.clue: He died a broken man, having lost his most prized business venture to Whitelaw Reid.

question.leadin: This speech states "Our war is not a war of conquest" and compares Cicero saving Rome from the Catiline conspiracy to Andrew Jackson saving America from the banks.
question.text: Name this speech that describes a free silver convention in Memphis, and compares proponents of that platform to the Crusaders following Peter the Hermit.
question.clue: This speech praises Thomas Benton's comparison of Andrew Jackson to Catiline, praising his actions "when he destroyed the bank conspiracy and saved America."

swap.leadin: Answer the following about wealthy American businessmen who also did philanthropy.
swap.text: This co-founder of the Standard Oil Company is often considered to be the wealthiest American of all time. He also founded the University of Chicago and a namesake university in Manhattan.
swap.clue: This man once owned the companies that became ExxonMobil and Chevron, and he clashed with Andrew Carnegie.

question.text: While in Quadling Country, the Cowardly Lion slays a large spider, representing trust-busting in this industry. The Granger Laws regulated prices in this industry, but were eventually struck down by cases like Wabash v. Illinois.
question.answerHtml: railroad industry [or the train industry, prompt on transportation industry]
question.clue: Richard Olney sent General Nelson Miles to put down another strike in this industry, which was stopped by Grover Cleveland due to a potential effect on mail delivery.

swap.text: This protestant group, famously led by Frances Willard, established those public drinking fountains and likewise advocated for social reforms, a ban on tobacco, as well as prohibition of alcohol.
swap.clue: The leader of this group gave a speech outlining the "Do Everything" policy of social reform to the "White Ribbon Army."

question.leadin: Secretary of the Treasury Abel Corbin attempted to end it by releasing some of the federal gold reserve.
question.text: What was this September 24, 1869 event, the culmination of two speculators' attempt to corner the gold market, which drove the price up to $13.50 an ounce?
question.clue: An important participant was Abel Corbin, who brought the architects of this scheme into high social circles.

swap.leadin: Prior to this engagement, explosives requisitions meant for mines by Patricio Montojo y Pasaron were instead sold by colonial authorities to various local construction companies.
swap.text: Identify this naval engagement that saw zero combat casualties for the US, despite Spain's attempts to attack George Dewey's flagship Olympia with Camara's Flying Relief Column.
swap.clue: The fighting took place around Sangley Point and commenced with the enemy's abandonment of its flagship, the Queen Christina.

question.leadin: Answer the following about protests by the American Indian Movement.
question.text: In 1973, AIM activists occupied this town in the Pine Ridge Reservation. In 1890, hundreds of Sioux were massacred near this South Dakota town's namesake creek as U.S. forces cracked down on the Ghost Dance.
question.clue: The Big Foot Memorial Riders end their path at this place, remembering an event that began due to Black Coyote's deafness.

swap.leadin: Seven policemen and four attendees were killed at this event after a pipe bomb was thrown at officers.
swap.text: This important event in labor history took place at a rally held at this site in Chicago.
swap.clue: Such was the fate of those convicted of inciting a riot at this Chicago square during an 1886 labor march.

question.text: This man dubbed the conflict "a splendid little war" and helped negotiate the Paris treaty as Secretary of State under McKinley. He's also known for writing some ballads about Pike County.
question.clue: In a speech before Congress, this man claimed that American intervention in East Asia was unnecessary.

swap.leadin: This essay praised Enoch Pratt, the founder of Baltimore's free public library system, and supported estate taxes as a "condemnation of the selfish millionaire's unworthy life."
swap.text: Name this 1889 essay advocating for philanthropy as a form of addressing inequality. Over 2,000 libraries were built using money donated by the author of this essay, Andrew Carnegie.
swap.clue: Andrew Carnegie argued that rich capitalists should use their fortune for the good of society in an essay which popularized the name of this social Darwinist ideology, which considers prosperity the reward for hard work and morality.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of disposable products in the United States.
question.text: This invention of William Painter was initially applied to another product with a foot-powered apparatus. This innovative disposable product allowed stores to stock certain items upright instead of on their sides.
question.answerHtml: bottle cap [or crown cap, or crown cork, or crown seal; prompt on cork]

swap.leadin: A Louisiana monopoly controlling these places was sued for limiting an asserted right to work.
swap.text: In a case named for these places, Associate Justice Samuel Miller ruled that the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment applied only to federal citizenship and not the states.
swap.answerHtml: slaughterhouses [accept meatpacking or meat processing factories or facilities; do not accept or prompt on “factories”]
swap.clue: This businesses that named a series of cases ruling that the Privileges and Immunities Clause protected only federal citizens.

question.leadin: According to lore, this event began when one participant mocked and humiliated the other for putting a skull on the wrong end of an Elasmosaurus skeleton.
question.text: Name this late 19th century rivalry between two U.S. paleontologists, to see who could discover more dinosaurs in the American west.
question.clue: That figure made further gains in this event by sending Samuel Williston to respond to a letter from two Union Pacific employees, thus gaining a huge foothold in Como Bluff.

swap.leadin: A history titled for this phrase's "origins" by C. Vann Woodward identifies its so-called "apostle," Daniel Augustus Tompkins, as a promoter of Social Darwinism in the Piedmont.
swap.text: Give this two-word phrase for an era typified by Vanderbilt's "Athenian" branding. This slogan was spread by boosters like the Constitution newspaper editor Henry W. Grady after the 1870s.
swap.answerHtml: “New South” [or “Emancipated South”; accept Origins of the New South, 1877–1913]
swap.clue: In a work titled for this period's "promise," Ed Ayers emphasized the important role of businessmen like Thomas A. Scott.

question.leadin: Name these exploring expeditions in the American West.
question.text: This geologist led a 10-year study of the 40th Parallel starting in Colorado, where he used his understanding of geology to blow the lid on the Diamond Hoax of 1872. Later in life, he passed as a black Pullman Porter named James Todd in order to marry Ada Copeland.

swap.leadin: This reform was reluctantly endorsed by George Cannon, who responded to it by saying "it behooveth me to require that work no more at the hands of those sons of men, but to accept of their offerings."
swap.text: Identify this reform promulgated by Wilford Woodruff in the 1890 Manifesto and the follow-up Second Manifesto after increased congressional scrutiny. A description is fine.
swap.answerHtml: ending polygamy in the Mormon Church [accept equivalent answers which indicate the end or ceasing of polygamy or plural marriage among Mormons]
swap.answer: ending polygamy in the Mormon Church
